facts.statement: The species Heteropetalus elegantulus was named in 1977 by Richard Lund from fossils found in the Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana.
facts.quote: Heteropetalus elegantulus was named in 1977 by paleontologist Richard Lund, based on several fossil specimens collected from the Serpukhovian-stage Bear Gulch Limestone of Fergus County, Montana.

facts.statement: Fossils of Heteropetalus are exceptionally well preserved, showing soft tissue details like eyes and a gill cover.
facts.quote: Known fossils of Heteropetalus are exceptionally well preserved, displaying details of the soft tissue anatomy such as the eyes and an opercular cover over the gills.

facts.statement: Heteropetalus reached a maximum length of 12 centimeters.
facts.quote: Heteropetalus grew to 12 cm in length.

facts.statement: The animal had a scaleless, torpedo-shaped body and a diphycercal tail fin.
facts.quote: The animal had a scaleless, fusiform body and a diphycercal tail fin.

facts.statement: Males had larger, modified dorsal fins with hook-like organs, indicating sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: Heteropetalus was sexually dimorphic, and the males had larger, modified dorsal fins which supported hook-like organs.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the hook-like structure on male dorsal fins functioned as a clasper to grab females during mating.
facts.quote: The hook-like structure on the dorsal fin of male Heteropetalus likely functioned as a clasper, and was used to grab females during mating.

facts.statement: Evidence of blood vessels in fossilized gills indicates these fish died by asphyxiation after being buried by mud.
facts.quote: The H. elegantulus buried by the mud then died by asphyxiation, as indicated by the blood vessels in their fossilized gills, and were preserved in exceptional detail.

facts.statement: Heteropetalus lived during the Serpukhovian stage, between 326.9 and 323.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Serpukhovian to Serpukhovian (326.9 to 323.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: Recent research places Heteropetalus in the order Debeeriiformes and family Debeeriidae based on similarities to Debeerius.
facts.quote: The most recent research by Richard Lund and Eileen Grogan has placed Heteropetalus in the order Debeeriiformes and the family Debeeriidae, due to similarities with the genus Debeerius.

facts.statement: Heteropetalus is classified as a member of the family Debeeriidae and the order Debeeriiformes.
facts.quote: Heteropetalus is a member of the family Debeeriidae and the order Debeeriiformes.
